analysis.one_liner: Requires secret-ballot elections for union representation and lets employers force hearings that delay those elections.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2024, referred to the Senate labor committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how union elections work. On paper, it requires that workers vote by secret ballot on whether to join a union. But federal union elections are already conducted by secret ballot under the National Labor Relations Board. The bill's real changes are procedural: it would require a hearing before any election could happen whenever an employer raises a dispute, and it would keep an election from being scheduled until the Board rules on those disputes — changes that would slow down and delay union elections. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing union organizing drives benefit most. The bill would give them a guaranteed pre-election hearing and would let any legal dispute they raise delay a union election, giving them more time to campaign against unionization before workers vote. Workers who oppose a union also gain from the explicit secret-ballot language, though that is already current practice.

how_it_helps.text: It writes a secret-ballot requirement into the National Labor Relations Act for union representation elections.
It blocks an election from taking place until the NLRB holds a hearing and rules on any disputes the employer raises about who is eligible to vote or other election issues.
It requires the Board to act on petitions within one month of filing.

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to organize a union pay the cost: mandatory hearings and dispute resolutions would delay elections, and delays favor employers who want to campaign against the union before the vote.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a mandatory pre-election hearing and keeps elections from proceeding until the Board rules on any legal dispute the employer raises, which would slow the election process and let employers delay a vote by filing challenges.
It imposes a rigid one-month deadline for the Board to act after a petition is filed, regardless of how complex the disputes are that the bill itself requires it to resolve first.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal—ensuring no worker is pressured how to vote—is achieved by the secret-ballot requirement, but NLRB elections are already secret ballots, so that part changes little in practice. The real change is the mandatory pre-election hearing and the one-month deadline: workers seeking a union would wait longer while employers litigate, and the delay gives employers time to campaign against the union. Weighing a symbolic guarantee against a slower, harder organizing process, the costs to workers' bargaining power outweigh the added protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee in April 2024 and never advanced; the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on April 16, 2024, with Senators Tuberville and Hagerty as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers opposed to union organizing keep the current status quo under NLRB rules; workers seeking faster union elections gained nothing, but also lost nothing that they had.

for.name: Sens. Tommy Tuberville and Bill Hagerty

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat supported the bill; it received no committee action or floor vote, so no broader voting record exists.

industries.note: The bill gives employers a guaranteed hearing and lets any legal dispute they raise hold up an election, giving them more time to campaign against unionization. Workers seeking a union would face a longer path to a contract.
Unions would face mandatory pre-election hearings and possible delays in every organizing drive, making it harder and slower to win representation elections.
